name: Steel Grey
lede: Steel Grey is a mid, faintly bluish grey named for the metal; it was already a stock term in the mineral colour lists that naturalists borrowed around 1800.

sections.title: A dark grey, or a mid one
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary glosses steel grey as simply a dark grey, and lists steel-black as a variant [1]. The swatch here is lighter than that: a mid, slightly bluish grey, with lightness 53 out of 100 and very little color [7]. The gap between the word and the swatch is the first thing to know about it. The word carries the idea of polished metal, and a flat patch of screen cannot.

The name is not new to any of the big color dictionaries. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives it a first record of 1493, a date we have not checked against an earlier source [7]. Ridgway's 1912 color standards and the 1955 ISCC-NBS tables also carry it, and the nearest ISCC-NBS category is bluish gray [7].

sections.title: Werner's grey with a lustre
sections.body:
As a term of the mineral trade, steel grey sits in Werner's series of greys, as passed on by Jameson in 1804 and by Syme in 1814 [4]. The run goes from lead-grey and bluish-grey through ash-grey to steel-grey, close to the dark end beside greyish-black [2].

Syme shows what the name carried. He described French grey as nearly the steel grey of Werner, but without the lustre [3]. So steel grey was a grey with a metallic sheen, a property that a naturalist could see in a specimen and a chart could only hint at [3].

sections.title: In pigments and cloth
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium uses the word for a pigment too [5]. Cobalt(III) oxide, made by heating precipitated cobalt hydroxide, is described there as a steel grey to black pigment, although commercial supplies are usually a mixture of two cobalt oxides [5].

In textiles, a reconstruction shown at Tate Modern in 2018 of Anni Albers's wall covering of 1929 for the Bernau trade union school looked grey-blue like steel, according to Finlay [6]. Both uses treat steel grey as a description of a look, not as a recipe.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of Steel Grey covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 441 works, or 1.85 per cent [8]. It is a color of light and mid tones: it plays a highlight role in 41 per cent of those paintings and a middle one in 51 per cent [8].

[[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] leads the painters. Fourteen of his 50 paintings in the archive carry it, 15 times the archive's rate, and Impressionism as a whole has 18 of 140, nearly seven times the average [8]. France supplies 108 of the 441 works [8]. The six paintings where it covers most include [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]]'s *Jungfrau*, a mountain watercolour of 1870 at 66 per cent, and [[painting:smk-KMS1658|Boys Bathing at Skagen]] by Krøyer, 1899, at 61 per cent [8]. The earliest example is [[painting:nga-9|The Madonna of Humility]] by Masaccio, 1423, at 9 per cent [8].

The word itself peaks in Google Books around 1808, within a few years of Jameson's 1804 mineral colour terms and Syme's 1814 book, though Ngram data cannot show cause [9]. It stands at 56 per cent of that level in 1800, about 20 per cent in 1840 and 13 per cent in 2000 [9]. As always, these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [8].

origin.first_recorded: 1493 per Maerz and Paul (1930), unchecked; in Werner's greys by 1804
origin.source: Baty, Nature's Palette, pp. 54, 173; ColorHub library

disambiguation.gloss: a bluer, more colorful relative; steel grey is almost neutral
